discovery: Invention and development of the optical lattice atomic clock

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori conceived the magic-wavelength optical lattice, which traps many neutral atoms without perturbing the clock transition. This combines the stability of large atomic ensembles with the accuracy of Lamb-Dicke confinement. Katori and Ye then turned the idea into working instruments. Their lattice clocks now reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and below, more than two orders of magnitude better than cesium standards. Ye's strontium clocks resolved the gravitational redshift across a single millimeter-scale atomic sample. Katori's transportable clocks measured height differences at Tokyo Skytree, which established relativistic geodesy. These clocks set new limits on variation of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark matter. They are driving the redefinition of the SI second and enable entanglement-enhanced metrology. The optical lattice clock is a new measurement paradigm: a laboratory probe of general relativity and new physics, and a practical sensor of Earth's gravity field.
